attributes.title: 6345a21b9192d80cc067714e

field_commentary.value: 和歌の浦は文飾として用いられる。和歌の浦から連想される語「藻塩草」を導き、藻塩草が波に洗われるように草子を洗うという表現。洗うことで書き込んだ墨が流れ、黒主の罪が露見する。
field_commentary.processed: <p>和歌の浦は文飾として用いられる。和歌の浦から連想される語「藻塩草」を導き、藻塩草が波に洗われるように草子を洗うという表現。洗うことで書き込んだ墨が流れ、黒主の罪が露見する。</p>

field_commentary_eng.value: Waka no ura is used as a poetic device. The word moshiogusa (seaweed), which is associated with Waka no ura,  expresses that like the seeweed which is washed by the waves of the sea the book (copy of the Man'yōshū) is washed. When drenched, the fresh ink on the paper is dissolved, revealing the plot of Kuronushi.

field_commentary.value: 『古今集仮名序』の小野小町評に「小野小町は古の衣通姫（そとほりひめ）の流れなり」とあるのを踏まえ、和歌の浦の玉津島神社の神として祀られる衣通姫の系譜を継いで和歌をたしなむ私（小野小町）が古歌を盗用する訳がないと反論する文脈で用いられる。古今集の注釈書『古今栄雅抄』によって衣通姫＝和歌の浦の玉津島明神＝和歌の神として神格化された説を踏まえる。

field_commentary_eng.value: Based on the commentary about Ono no Komachi in  the Kokinshū kana-jo, "Ono no Komachi is a modern Princess Sotōri"(English translation by Rodd, Laurel R. (1984): p.45), it is used in the context of arguing that "I" (Ono no Komachi), a waka poet and descendant of Princess Sotōri, who is enshrined as the deity of Tamatsushima Shrine in Waka no ura, would not plagiarize ancient poetry. According to the Kokin eigashō, a commentary of the Kokinshū, this is based on the theory that Princess Sotōri was deified as the deity of Tamatsushima in Waka no ura and with this as the god of waka poetry.

field_commentary.value: 『古今集仮名序』の大伴黒主評に「その様賤しし、いはゞ薪を負へる山人の花の蔭に休めるがごとし」とある、そのままの様子でシテが現れる。ここでの「和歌の浦」は、和歌の文飾としての使用。平良直の和歌「かひもなき/和歌の浦わの/藻塩草/かく置くまでを/思い出にせん」（『続後拾遺集』・巻16・1083番歌）をふまえ、大伴黒主が老いても熱心に読んだ和歌について、『古今集仮名序』で喩えて書かれたことが世間に知られているという文脈で用いる。

field_commentary_eng.value: In the Kokinshū kana-jo, the commentary about the poet Ōtomo no Kuronushi is as follows: "Ōtomo no Kuronushi’s songs are rustic in form; they are like a mountaineer with a bundle of firewood on his back resting in the shade of the blossoms" (English translation by Rodd, Laurel R. (1984): p.46). The  appearance of the shite is in accordance with this description. “Waka no ura" here is used as a poetic device in waka poems. The waka poem by Taira no Yoshinao, "Everything is in vain, the drying seaweed in the bay of Waka, the time before it was laid down, I want to remember that” (Shokugoshūi wakashū, vol. 16, poem no. 1083) refers to the well known context of the preface to the Kokinwakashū where Ōtomo no Kuronushi is mentioned as having written waka poems with great enthusiasm even in his old age.

field_scene_description_eng.value: When a vassal (waki) of the current emperor goes to see the mountain cherry blossoms of Shiga, he meets an old lumberjack (shite, actually the spirit of Otomo no Kuronushi) resting in the shade of the flowers, carrying firewood on his back, which point at the cherry blossoms. As the vassal, who thinks that the lumberjack looks just like Ōtomo no Kuronushi, addresses him, the man replies that he is just a mountain man of low status.
